title: One Sacrifice for All Time: Draw Near and Hold Fast
summary: The law's sacrifices, repeated year after year, could never perfect worshipers or take away sins. Quoting Psalm 40, the author shows that Christ came to do God's will and offered his body once for all, then sat down, having perfected those being sanctified, as Jeremiah's new covenant promised. Therefore believers should draw near to God, hold fast their hope, and keep meeting together. A solemn warning follows against deliberately rejecting Christ, and then an encouragement to remember their earlier endurance and not throw away their confidence.
story: This chapter brings the central argument of the letter to its conclusion and turns it toward life. Verses 1-18 complete the teaching on Christ's sacrifice begun in chapter 8, closing with the same promise from Jeremiah 31 with which it began: sins remembered no more. From verse 19 the tone shifts to exhortation. Because of all that Christ has done, the readers can approach God and must hold on together. The fourth warning passage (verses 26-31) parallels the warning of chapter 6, and the chapter ends by recalling the readers' past courage and quoting Habakkuk on living by faith, which leads directly into the great chapter on faith that follows.
historical:
Verses 32-34 give a rare glimpse of the readers' history. In their early days as believers, soon after they "were in the light", they suffered public abuse, some were imprisoned, others stood by the prisoners, and they accepted the seizure of their property with joy. Scholars who locate the readers in Rome often connect this with the emperor Claudius's expulsion of Jews from Rome around AD 49, which the Roman historian Suetonius links to disturbances over a certain Chrestus, commonly taken as a garbled reference to Christ, and which Acts 18:2 also mentions. Imprisoned people in the Roman world depended on friends and family to bring food and supplies, and visiting prisoners could itself mark someone as a sympathizer.

The author's statement that the old sacrifices were offered year after year and served as an annual reminder of sins (verses 1-3) suggests to many readers that the temple was still standing. Others note that he is describing the tabernacle system as Scripture presents it and that the argument would work either way.
cultural:
Priests in Israel stood while they served; there was no chair in the tabernacle for them to sit on, because their work was never finished. The contrast of verses 11-12 is visual: every priest stands day after day, but Christ sat down. A seated priest meant a completed sacrifice.

The call to meet together (verse 25) assumes the practice of regular assembly, probably in homes. The word used is related to synagogue, the Jewish gathering, and the author warns that some had begun to stop attending, perhaps from fear of being identified with the movement, perhaps from fatigue. The losses listed in verse 34 were real: confiscation of goods could follow a legal charge or simply mob action, and it left families without a livelihood. The author reminds the readers that they had accepted it because they knew they had "a better and permanent possession".
literary: The chapter has three sections. Verses 1-18 contrast the repeated sacrifices of the law with the single offering of Christ, supported by Psalm 40:6-8 (verses 5-7), which the author interprets phrase by phrase in verses 8-10, and by Jeremiah 31:33-34 (verses 16-17). The quotation of Psalm 40 follows the Greek Old Testament, which reads "a body You prepared for Me" where the Hebrew has an image of ears opened to hear, and the author builds his point on that wording: Christ's obedience was offered in a body. Verses 19-25 form one long sentence of exhortation with three calls: let us draw near (faith), let us hold fast (hope), and let us consider one another (love). Verses 26-39 combine warning (verses 26-31), remembrance (verses 32-34), and encouragement (verses 35-39), closing with Habakkuk 2:3-4, also from the Greek version.

outline.t: The law's sacrifices cannot take away sins
Psalm 40: I have come to do your will
One sacrifice for all time and a seated priest
Draw near, hold fast, and meet together
Remember your former courage and live by faith

doctrines.note: Christ's single offering accomplishes what countless sacrifices could not: "by a single offering He has made perfect for all time those who are being sanctified" (verse 14). Once sins are forgiven, no further offering is needed (verse 18).
Believers draw near to God together, and they are responsible to spur one another on to love and good deeds and not to abandon their gatherings (verses 24-25). Perseverance is a communal task.

The chapter speaks soberly of "a fearful expectation of judgment" for those who deliberately reject Christ, grounding it in Deuteronomy 32:35-36. The same God who forgives completely also judges his people.
Faith is the posture of the righteous one who lives by it and does not shrink back (verses 38-39). It looks forward to the promise and endures in the meantime.

words.note: Ephapax, once for all, once and never again. It is a key word in Hebrews (7:27, 9:12, 10:10). The sacrifice of Christ is not only once in time but once in sufficiency; nothing needs to be added or repeated.

Parresia, confidence or boldness, originally the freedom of a citizen to speak openly in the assembly. Believers now have parresia to enter the Most Holy Place by the blood of Jesus (verse 19), and they are urged not to throw it away (verse 35).

Hekousios, deliberately or willingly. It qualifies the sinning in verse 26. The law distinguished unintentional sins, for which sacrifice was provided, from sins committed defiantly (Numbers 15:27-31). The warning concerns a willful, persistent rejection, not ordinary failures.

Hupomone, endurance or perseverance, the ability to remain under a load without giving up. The readers need it to receive what God has promised (verse 36), and chapter 12 will call them to run with it.

christ: This chapter shows Christ as the obedient Son who came into the world to do God's will, the one sacrifice that makes all others obsolete, and the priest who sat down because his work was done. His body was the new and living way through the curtain into God's presence (verse 20). He now waits at God's right hand until his enemies are made his footstool, echoing Psalm 110:1. And he is the one "who is coming" and "will not delay" (verse 37). Faith, hope, and love in the church all rest on what he has already accomplished.

hard.q: What does it mean that "no further sacrifice for sins remains" for those who deliberately go on sinning?
hard.a:
Verses 26-31 are, with 6:4-6, one of the letter's most feared passages. The context shows what kind of sin is meant: trampling the Son of God, treating the blood of the covenant as unholy, and insulting the Spirit of grace (verse 29). This is a deliberate, persistent repudiation of Christ, not the ordinary sins with which every believer struggles. The logic is that Christ's sacrifice is the only one; to reject it is to have no other.

Interpreters read the passage through the same frameworks as chapter 6. Reformed interpreters hold that those who finally reject Christ in this way show they were never truly regenerate, though they belonged to the community; the phrase "the blood of the covenant that sanctified him" is read as describing the outward setting apart of a member of the covenant community. Arminian and Wesleyan interpreters take it as describing genuine believers who can fall away through willful apostasy. Others hold that the warning is a real means God uses to keep his people from that end, and some Free Grace interpreters read the judgment as temporal discipline or loss of reward rather than eternal condemnation. Catholic and Orthodox interpreters read it as a warning about mortal sin and apostasy, from which repentance is still possible by God's grace though not by any other sacrifice.

The author immediately adds, "But we are not of those who shrink back" (verse 39). His purpose is not to drive anxious believers to despair but to keep a drifting congregation from walking away from the only hope they have.

questions: Christ sat down because his work was finished. Where are you still living as if you had to keep offering something to God to be accepted?
The author tells believers to consider how to spur one another on to love and good deeds. Who has done that for you, and whom could you encourage?
The readers once endured suffering with joy but were now losing heart. What helps a person recover the courage of earlier days?
